question: Which statement best describes React.memo?
options: Caches a function's identity across renders so a memoized child receiving it as a prop doesn't see a 'new' function every time. It is exactly useMemo(() => fn, deps) specialized for functions. Without it, an inline arrow passed to a React.memo child creates a fresh reference each render and breaks the memoization you were trying to achieve.

A higher-order component that skips re-rendering when the new props are shallowly (referentially) equal to the previous ones. It only helps when a component is genuinely expensive AND its props stay stable across the parent's re-renders — a single inline object, array, or function prop defeats it entirely. You can pass a custom areEqual(prev, next) comparator, but that is easy to get subtly wrong.

React's memoization compares by identity (===), not structure, because reference checks are O(1) while deep comparison would be expensive. Primitives compare by value and are stable, but {} === {}, [] === [], and (()=>{}) === (()=>{}) are all false — so objects, arrays, and functions created during render are brand-new references every time. Nearly every 'my memo doesn't work' bug is a referential-equality problem; the fix is useMemo/useCallback or hoisting a constant to module scope.

Caches the result of an expensive computation, recomputing only when a dependency changes by reference. Its two jobs are: avoid redoing costly work (sorting/filtering large data) on every render, and keep a derived object/array's reference stable so a downstream React.memo boundary can actually skip. It does not stop the current component from rendering, and React may discard the cache, so treat it as a hint, not a guarantee.

question: Which statement best describes useMemo?
options: Rendering thousands of DOM nodes makes layout and paint expensive; virtualization mounts only the rows currently in (and just around) the viewport, keeping the DOM node count bounded regardless of dataset size. You track scroll position, compute the visible index range from row height, and use a full-height spacer so the scrollbar stays correct, with a small overscan to avoid blank flashes. In production prefer a library like react-window or react-virtuoso for variable heights and edge cases.

question: Which statement best describes List virtualization (windowing)?
options: Memoization isn't free: every memo boundary adds a prop comparison and every useMemo/useCallback stores values and checks dependencies, so blanket use can be net-negative and harder to read. The discipline is to measure first with the React DevTools Profiler (render counts, durations, why-did-this-render) and Web Vitals (INP, LCP, CLS), then optimize the proven hot path — don't optimize what isn't slow.
